newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Howard briefs Australian cabinet on native title.
newsitem.headline: Howard briefs Australian cabinet on native title.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Tuesday briefed cabinet on Aboriginal native title but the government has still not finalised a policy on the issue, which farmers and miners say is damaging their industry.
"The prime minister briefed cabinet on the Wik issue," the official told Reuters, referring to the Wik case in which the High Court extended its 1992 invention of native title to pastoral leases.
"There was a detailed discussion," the official said on condition of anonymity as the cabinet met in Brisbane.
The native title issue has created strong tensions in the ruling Liberal-National coalition, with the rural-based National party urging strong action to protect farmers' interests.
But cabinet did not finalise a policy on Tuesday and the official said Howard would talk again with farmers and aborigines.
"The prime minister is planning to have further discussion with interested parties over the coming week," he said.
The High Court ruled in December that Aborigines might still have some indeterminate rights to use land that the government had leased to pastoralists, contrary to previous assumptions.

Because the extent of the Aborigines' rights are uncertain, farmers say they cannot make business decisions until the government clarifies the issue with legislation, and they are calling for statutory abolition of native title on the leases.
Much of the Australian mining industry also operates on current or former pastoral leases.
Earlier on Tuesday the National Farmers Federation claimed that almost two-thirds of Australians supported farmers' push to be protected against native title.

"Obviously, our message -- for the restoration of the rights of farmers -- cut through the media clutter and was accepted by our target audience," federation executive director Wendy Craik said in a speech.
The federation has pushed its cause with controversial television advertisements on the issue, one of them showing a black child beating a white child in a competitive game.

The whole concept of native title, which the Wik case merely extended, was invented in 1992's Mabo case, which caused protracted and heated political debate eventually finalised when the then Labor created a system to handle land claims.
The government could ask federal parliament to simply abolish native title but would find the move practically difficult because it would appear racist and because compensation would have to be paid.
Howard, who has already missed a promise to produce a policy by Easter, has said that if primary producers and Aborigines cannot agree on the issue then he will simply impose a policy on them.
